title: Developing stratified pathways to advance readiness in children for school 2
official: Mapping unmet needs and support of families between neonatal discharge and school entry: a UK cross-sectional survey with nested qualitative interviews (SPARCS2)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Every year, over 70,000 babies in the UK are cared for in a neonatal unit, including neonatal intensive care units (NICU). There are many reasons that babies need this care, including being born prematurely, having a birth injury, or other health conditions needing extra support. As medical care improves, more babies who need neonatal care are surviving and growing up to start school.
We know that some babies who spend time in NICU are more likely to face challenges as they grow, with their language, movement, thinking skills, or emotional development. Their families often also face extra pressures, such as their child's ongoing health needs, parents' mental health, or financial and housing difficulties.
Our earlier SPARCS study found that at least one in three children who had been in NICU was not fully ready for school by age 5 years. When we brought together parents, health professionals, and researchers to discuss this, everyone agreed that families currently have no clear pathway to get their child's development checked and supported before school starts.
SPARCS2 aims to change this. We want to find out which children and families need additional support, what support is needed, and how it can be provided at the right times to improve the experiences of future families after neonatal care across the UK.

Who can participate?
Parents and carers aged 16 years or over of a child who was admitted to any neonatal unit in the UK at any point from 2020 and onwards. Parents whose child has died are also welcome to take part if they wish.

What does the study involve?
The study has two parts, and families can take part in one or both.
First, around 500 parents will complete an online survey, which takes about 5 minutes. The survey asks about the family's background, the child's neonatal stay and how they are doing now, and the family's experience of getting support since leaving the neonatal unit. There are also open questions where parents can describe their experience in their own words. The survey is available in English, Polish, Romanian, Arabic, Punjabi and Urdu. Parents answer only the questions that apply to their own situation, and can skip any question or stop at any point.
Second, around 30 parents will take part in a longer, more detailed interview lasting about 30 to 60 minutes, held online by video call at a time that suits them. Interviews are conducted in English. Parents can ask to be contacted about an interview at the end of the survey, or can contact the study team directly after seeing the study advertised. We will choose parents from a range of backgrounds, social circumstances, and regions of the UK, so that we hear a wide range of views. Interviews are audio recorded and typed up, with names and other identifying details removed.
This study is conducted entirely online. Families can take part from anywhere in the UK, so no travel or hospital visit is needed. Parents who complete the survey receive a £10 voucher, and parents who take part in an interview receive a £30 voucher, as a thank you for their time. Data are stored securely at the University of Cambridge and are analysed without names attached, so that individual families cannot be recognised.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Taking part will not change the care that a family or child receives. The main benefit is helping to shape better support for families who need neonatal care in the future, and parents have told us that having their experience heard matters to them.
There are no physical risks. Some parents may find it upsetting to think back to their baby's time in neonatal care, or to answer questions about their child's health or, for some families, their child's death. Parents can skip any question, take a break, or stop at any point without giving a reason, and will still receive their voucher. Warnings appear before questions that some parents may find difficult, and details of organisations that can offer support are given to everyone taking part.

Where is the study run from? 
University of Cambridge (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
December 2026 to July 2028

Who is funding the study? 
UK Research and Innovation

Who is the main contact?
Prof. Catherine Aiken, cema2@cam.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Parents or primary caregivers, aged 16 years or over, of a child who required admission to a neonatal unit (any level of neonatal care, not restricted to tertiary NICU) in the UK, who are willing and able to give informed consent.

NICU admission disproportionately affects families of Black and Asian ethnicity and families experiencing financial hardship, housing insecurity, or other social adversity, and as such, the study has been designed to actively support participation from underrepresented groups:
1. Recruitment will run through multiple parallel channels (social media, NHS/charity partner organisations, community and faith organisations) rather than a single route, to avoid systematic under-reach of any one group.
2. Participant-facing materials (information sheets, survey, consent) will be written in the top 5 most widely spoken languages in the UK and reviewed for accessibility.
3. The survey and interview will be available in formats compatible with screen readers, and participants may request a version read aloud to them or completed with support from a family member or the study team.
4. Purposive sampling for the interview phase will explicitly track ethnicity, region, and socioeconomic proxy to ensure the interview participants are not skewed toward digitally-engaged, high-resource families.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Aged under 16 years
2. Lacks capacity to consent
3.1. For survey participants: unable to understand and complete the survey in one of the languages in which validated study materials are available
3.2. For interview participants: insufficient spoken English to participate meaningfully in an interview without an interpreter
4. Neonatal unit admissions over 6 years ago (i.e., before 2020)
